title: 2 John

stories.title: 📜 2 John
summaryBullets: The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth — and not I alone, but also all who know the truth — (1:1).
because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever: (1:2).
Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love. (1:3).
I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us. (1:4).
And now I urge you, dear lady — not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning — that we love one another. (1:5).
And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love. (1:6).
For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist. (1:7).
Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded. (1:8).
Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son. (1:9).
If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. (1:10).
Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds. (1:11).
I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete. (1:12).
The children of your elect sister send you greetings. (1:13).
crossRefs: John 14:6: Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life.
3 John 1:4: Joy that children walk in the truth.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּבְחֶרֶת (hāʾiššāh hannibḥéreṯ, sense), Greek: ἐκλεκτῇ κυρίᾳ (eklektē kyría, NT), Aramaic: אתתא בחירתא (ʾettatā baḥīrtā)
translationNotes.note: Likely refers to a specific woman believer and her household, though some interpret it figuratively of a church; literally means 'chosen lady.'

stories.keyTakeaway: John greets the elect lady and her children with love in truth, affirming grace, mercy, and peace, and rejoicing in their faithful walk.

intro:
2 John was written by John the apostle, who identifies himself in verse 1 as "the elder" (Greek ho presbyteros, "the elder one"), a self-designation appropriate to John's status as the last surviving apostle and the senior pastor of the churches of the Roman province of Asia at the close of the first century AD. The letter was composed at Ephesus around AD 85-95, during the same period in which John wrote 1 John, 3 John, and (slightly later) Revelation. The letter is addressed to "the elect lady and her children" (verse 1). The "elect lady" (Greek eklektē kyria) has been understood in two main ways within Bible-affirming tradition: most commentators take "lady" as a personification of a local church and "her children" as its members, a reading supported by the parallel closing greeting from "the children of your elect sister" in verse 13 (most likely a sister congregation in another city, most plausibly the church in Ephesus where John was based); an alternative reading takes the lady as a literal Christian woman (possibly named Kyria, which can also be read as a personal name). The brevity of the letter (only thirteen verses, one of the two shortest books in the New Testament along with 3 John) and the use of "house" in verse 10 fit either reading. For the full biographical sketch of John the apostle (Galilean fisherman, son of Zebedee, brother of James, the inner three, the disciple Jesus loved, caretaker of Mary, pillar of the Jerusalem church, Ephesian elder, exiled to Patmos under Domitian, died in extreme old age around AD 100 as the only apostle not martyred), see the introduction to the Gospel of John. The early church unanimously attributed 2 John to John the apostle, with Irenaeus (c. AD 180, Against Heresies 1.16.3 and 3.16.8) quoting 2 John 11 by name as the work of "John, the disciple of the Lord."

The historical setting is the same as 1 John: the city of Ephesus and the surrounding churches of the Roman province of Asia in the closing decades of the first century, with the same proto-Gnostic and docetic teachers (associated especially with the Ephesian teacher Cerinthus) spreading the same heresy that denied Jesus' coming "in the flesh." 2 John 7 echoes 1 John 4:1-3 directly: "Many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist." 2 John addresses the same crisis with a particular practical concern about hospitality. In the first-century Christian world, traveling teachers depended on church hospitality for food and lodging as they moved from city to city; respectable believers were expected to receive these traveling teachers into their homes and to send them on with provisions for the next stage of their journey. The Ephesian docetic teachers were exploiting this expected hospitality to spread their false doctrine from house to house and church to church. John writes to instruct the elect lady (and through her, the church she represents) that the obligation of Christian hospitality does NOT extend to teachers who deny the incarnation: "If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting, for whoever greets him takes part in his wicked works" (2 John 10-11). The Roman emperor at the time of writing was Domitian (AD 81-96), whose imperial-cult persecution of Christians in Asia would soon send John himself into exile on Patmos.

2 John is the sixty-third book of the Christian Bible, the twenty-fourth book of the New Testament, and the fifth of the seven General Epistles. At thirteen verses (one chapter), it is tied with 3 John as one of the two shortest books in the New Testament; Obadiah (twenty-one verses) is the shortest book in the Old Testament. The earliest surviving manuscripts include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD); Papyrus 74 (P74, 7th century) is another important early witness. The letter's central truths are condensed: truth and love are inseparable (verses 1-6: "I rejoiced greatly to find some of your children walking in the truth... And now I ask you, dear lady, not as though I were writing you a new commandment, but the one we have had from the beginning, that we love one another"); doctrinal fidelity matters because denying the incarnation severs one from God himself (verse 9: "Everyone who goes on ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God; whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son"); and Christian hospitality must not be deployed in service of heresy (verses 10-11). The letter closes with John's intention to visit in person (verse 12: "Though I have much to write to you, I would rather not use paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete").
